intro: A skateboard looks simple: a board, two trucks, four wheels. Look closer and every part is an engineering decision. Seven thin plies of maple are glued and pressed into a curve. Wheels are cast from liquid chemicals and rated with a hardness gauge. Eight small steel bearings let those wheels spin thousands of times a minute. Ramps are curves drawn from circles, and their radius decides how hard a rider's legs must work.

This unit follows the engineer's way of thinking. You will see how layered wood and concave make a deck stiff without making it heavy, why a soft wheel wins on a rough street and loses at a smooth park, and why the ABEC number on a bearing box is about precision, not speed. Then you will design a ramp: use geometry to find its top angle and footprint, energy to predict a rider's speed, and centripetal acceleration to predict how heavy the rider will feel at the bottom.

By the end you will be able to explain the trade-offs behind a skateboard setup, read wheel and bearing labels correctly, and carry out a full ramp design calculation with each step shown. You will also know how ramps are framed and built safely, and how to check a design against the people who will ride it.
bigQuestion: How do engineers use materials, geometry and physics to build boards and ramps that fit the people who ride them?

test.q: What is most often used to make a skateboard deck?
test.why: Most decks are seven thin plies of hard maple glued and pressed.

test.q: Why do some plies in a deck run across the board?
choices: to keep the deck from splitting along the grain
test.why: Cross plies hold the lengthwise fibers together so the deck resists splitting.

test.q: A deck is made 20 percent thicker. About how much stiffer does it get?

test.why: Higher numbers on the A scale are harder, so 101A is hardest.

test.q: Why does a soft wheel ride smoothly on rough ground?
choices: it squashes over bumps with a larger contact patch
test.why: A soft wheel deforms over pebbles and cracks and spreads bumps over a larger contact patch.

test.q: What problem do riser pads help prevent?
test.why: Riser pads lift the deck so large wheels do not touch it in turns.

test.q: What does a higher ABEC grade mean?
test.why: ABEC classes set limits on size and running accuracy; higher means tighter limits.

test.q: In a bearing, why does friction stay low?
choices: the races are made of wood
the balls roll between the races instead of sliding
test.why: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.

test.q: A 54 mm wheel (circumference 0.170 m) rolls at 6.8 m/s. How many turns per second?
A curve has radius 3.0 m and the ramp is 1.5 m tall. What is cos θ at the top?
With no friction, what speed does a rider reach after a 0.9 m drop?
A 70 kg rider moves at 4 m/s at the bottom of a 2 m radius curve. What is the normal force?
Why does a tighter curve feel harder on the legs?
choices: a smaller radius means a larger v²/r and less time to react
test.why: Felt weight is 1 + 2h ÷ r, so a smaller radius raises the force, and the curve passes faster.

test.q: When a rider pumps, where do they press up through the legs?
choices: through the bottom of the curve
in the middle of the flat bottom
test.why: Pressing up where the ramp pushes hardest, at the bottom of the curve, adds energy.

test.q: Which step makes a ramp's surface safer for wheels and knee pads?
test.why: Countersunk screws sit below the surface so nothing catches on them.

write.prompt: Design a mini ramp for a group you know. Choose a height and a radius, then show each step of your arithmetic for the top angle, the curve's footprint, the speed at the bottom and the felt weight there. Explain one trade-off you made and why it fits your riders.
tips: Use cos θ = 1 − h ÷ r for the top angle and r × sin θ for the footprint.
Use v = √(2gh) with g = 9.8 m/s² for the speed at the bottom.
Use 1 + 2h ÷ r for how many times their weight riders feel.
Say who the riders are and how your numbers suit them.
Name one safety step in building or checking the ramp.
